newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK PARLT REJECTS DRAFT ON PRESIDENTIAL VOTE.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK PARLT REJECTS DRAFT ON PRESIDENTIAL VOTE.

text.p: Slovak parliament rejected on Wednesday an opposition draft law on direct presidential elections, with Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's ruling party claiming it could open a Pandora's box of constitutional votes.

The proposal to change the constitution to allow the direct election of the president by citizens and not parliament was defeated by the governing coalition majority by 62 against to 46 in favour and 37 abstentions.
The vote, however, does not effect the opposition's drive to force a referendum on the subject through a petition by citizens.

In February, opposition parties collected some 500,000 signatures under a petition calling on President Michal Kovac to call a refendum on the issue. Kovac is expected to do so by the end of the week.

Opponents to the referendum have warned that if a constitional change to allow direct presidential elections was approved, it could lead to further referenda on subjects such as re-imposition of the death penalty.
"I can assure and warn you that a second or third referendum of this kind will approve the death penalty regardless of all legal and international barriers," Peter Brnak of the HZDS told parliament.

The governing coalition, led by HZDS, and the opposition appear unable to agree on a common presidential candidate and neither is able to garner the three-fifths majority necessary in the 150-seat house to push through their own choice in a vote scheduled for March 1998.

If such a stalemate occurs, Meciar would assume presidential powers until a new parliament is elected at a general vote planned for the autumn of 1998, when the body would again have to propose a presidential candidate.

Following Wednesday's vote, parliament formally closed its session and began another extraordinary session to debate a law on the suspension of bank priovatisation to the end of 2003, which Kovac returned to parliament for revision.
The government has said the bill could jeopardize Slovakia's ambitions for membership in the OECD.
"OECD representatives have warned that adoption of this law could become a serious obstacle in the process of the acceptance of Slovakia into this prestigious organisation," Kozlik told parliament.
